In this vein, I’d like to set the stage with the short-term outlook for this year and follow-up with
some ways to foster long-term growth.

In response, the Fed tightened policy during 1994 to suppress inflationary pressures that were
building up in the economy and to put us back on a trajectory more in line with a rate of
sustainable growth.

The Consumer Price Index rose 23⁄4 percent, the fourth straight year at under three percent, and
the unemployment rate was 5.6% ,its lowest sustained level in five years.

In December and, again, in Januar y, we decided to ease the federal funds rate — 1⁄4 of a
percentage point each time.

The December decision was based on the positive outlook for inflation and some concerns about
the risks of prolonged sluggishness.

a. Harsh weather had disrupted normal economic patterns.
b. The economy seemed to be softening, but that appeared to be due to temporary factors —
like the weather.
c. In fact, a number of fundamental factors indicated the economy was basically on track
for sustained growth.
d. The FOMC decided it was appropriate to ease monetary policy slightly as a form of
insurance against the risk of below potential economic performance.
(i) And, it didn’t seem that this would boost inflationary pressures.
4.

B. First, consumer spending. Consumer spending accounts for about two-thirds of GDP so it’s an area
we watch closely.
1.

Consumer spending growth was moderate during 1995, at about 2% on a fourth quarter-tofourth quarter basis.

Here are a couple of considerations in looking at consumer spending for 1996.
a. There’s some concern that consumers may cut back on their spending because they’ve
accumulated too much debt.
(i) We do not think that will happen.
b. Debt numbers are up because credit cards are easier to obtain and use.
c. Credit cards have also become increasingly available to those in lower income classes,
who previously did not typically have such ready access to credit, a very important
change for the economy.
d. Furthermore, people have become much more likely to use credit to buy things like gas
and groceries.
(i) Such convenience credit is typically repaid within the next billing cycle, so it
shouldn’t put a crimp in spending.
(ii) In fact, lower interest rates and better terms have made it easier for consumers to
service their debt.
e. Nevertheless, recent increases in interest rates could impact consumers ability to service
their debt.
f. Unanticipated economic slowdowns may impact new users of credit more significantly
than more seasoned users of credit.
g. Yet it is important to note that interest rates continue to be lower than they were a year ago.

C. Given that we are five years into the current economic expansion, some would suggest concern
there’s likely to be less pent-up demand for consumer goods, as durable goods purchases tend to
rise more sharply in earlier stages of expansions.
1.

Given a healthy income picture and fairly steady employment growth, we expect consumer
spending to increase about the same or slightly faster in 1996 than it did last year.

It is clear that labor markets are tight.
a. The national unemployment rate averaged 5.6 percent during 1995, the lowest sustained
level in five years.

Here in the Midwest, our unemployment rates have been lower than the national figures. Despite
this, we haven’t seen much systematic pressure for larger wage gains
a. When unemployment was this low in the past, businesses had to increase wages more
aggressively to attract workers.
b. These wage pressures are of interest to the Fed because they could trigger inflationary
pressures.
c. Don’t get me wrong. Wage increases are good... as long as they are accompanied by
increases in productivity.
(i) If they’re not, then we’re likely to see price inflation rise. Nobody is helped by
higher wages when prices are increasing.
d. Many have noted that subdued pressure for wage increases may be due in part to job
insecurity.
(i) Presumably this results, in part, from the jarring changes taking place in many
industries – particularly highly publicized downsizing at many large corporations
and perhaps a greater move to outsourcing and the use of temporary workers.
e. Labor unions seem to be also increasingly focusing on job security in contract negotiations, and we’ve seen an unusually low level of strikes. In 1995, work stoppages
were at a fifty-year low.

I anticipate that we’ll have growth of two percent or slightly higher for the year.
a. That’s approximately the growth our economy can sustain without sparking an increase
in inflation.

The consumer price index should come in below three percent, and the unemployment rate
should end the year at close to its current levels.

C. Some commentators have expressed concern about the recent increases in prices of certain basic
commodities such as corn, wheat, and crude oil.
1. Supply and political factors seem to have contributed to these dramatic increases.
2. Thus far these price changes do not appear to have had a significant impact on underlying
inflation trends, but we are continuing to monitor such developments.
3. Another area of potential concern is the increase in longer-term interest rates we’ve seen
over the past few months and the potential impact on industries such as housing. In part,
this increase reflects the stronger economy in the first quarter as well as expectations of
higher inflation.
4. In my view, the slowdown in balanced budget negotiations between the Congress and the
Administration also contributed to the rise in interest rates.
a. Though a two percent real GDP growth rate isn’t exciting, it sure isn’t bad.
(i) An economy that grows consistently at that rate can achieve excellent results over
the long haul.
b. As far as we at the Fed are concerned, steady, healthy growth is the ideal.
(i) Those slam dunks look great, but you’ll have trouble winning if you’ve neglected to
practice free throws and defense.
(ii) It’s attention to the basics that set you up for steady, sustained progress over time.
V. And that brings me to the last area I want to touch on: how to foster sustainable economic growth
and a better standard of living for the long run.
A. This, after all, is the Fed’s basic goal.

The first is price stability and the second is an adequate savings rate.
a. They reinforce one another.

Over the last 15 years, we’ve made significant progress keeping inflation in check.
a. However, I believe the savings rate must be higher than it is if we want to grow at faster
rates.

D. As I noted earlier, growing at our long term potential rate is not exciting.
1.

Many people would like to see the economy grow faster even if it means higher inflation.
a. They ask, “Wouldn’t it be worth a few points on the consumer price index to put thousands
of people back to work?”
(i) Unfortunately, it’s not that simple.

Economic growth is determined by labor force growth and productivity growth.
a. The best way to improve our standard of living is to increase productivity.
(i) That allows for higher incomes that will not be eaten away by rising prices.
b. The best way to lower our standard of living is to try to grow faster than our labor force
and productivity, triggering a wage-price spiral and adding even more points to the CPI.
(i) The end result is high inflation and slow growth.

We need higher levels of investment. And to increase investment, we need a higher level of
savings since savings is the source of investment funds.
United States averaged close to 20 percent of GNP.

During the 1980s, net savings — which includes household, business and government savings—
fell to an average of three percent of GNP, well below net fixed investment of about five percent.
This was occurring at the same time that Germany and Japan had much higher savings and
investment rates.

Given the importance of savings and investment, it’s easy to see why ensuring price stability is the
best way to foster maximum sustainable growth.
1.

It is important to use sound policy to stop inflation before it gets out of hand.

High inflation distorts decisions. People expend too much of their resources to protect themselves from price increases.
a. They make fewer long-term investments because they expect their return will be eaten
away by inflation.
b. They spend more on consumer goods short-term because inflation will reduce the value
of their dollars.

This inflation mentality creeps in and affects decisions. We’ve seen that happen.
a. Stable and low inflation leads to sound decisions and more efficient allocation of
resources.
b. It encourages savings and investment which, in turn, foster productivity increases.
(i) And this achieves the Federal Reserve’s mission — a goal that we all share: healthy
sustainable growth and a higher standard of living for us all.
